meta.title: samogrow by Nombox — DIY AI herb garden
meta.description: samogrow by Nombox — an open-source (MIT), AI-run indoor herb garden you build from commodity parts. Starts at ~$255 (manual), ~$280 automated core, to ~$335 with add-ons. A camera checks the plants, smart plugs control light and water, and Telegram reports. No vendor subscription and no proprietary pods; recurring cost is $3–7/mo in Claude API calls plus ~$35/yr in commodity consumables. Runs on a machine you already keep on; try it in mock mode with zero hardware.
hero.eyebrow: A service you can read · open source · it feeds you
hero.lede: You already keep a machine on 24/7. Give it one more job. samogrow runs a herb garden from a camera, two smart plugs, and a Claude API key — open source (MIT), no pods, no subscription.

how.title: How it works
how.sub: The garden is three off-the-shelf Wi-Fi gadgets — two smart plugs and a camera — with nothing to maintain. The brain is nombox, a small TypeScript/Bun service (@anthropic-ai/sdk for vision, grammY for Telegram, everything in one config.json) that runs on a machine you already leave on: it pulls a photo, asks Claude what to do, switches the light and pump plugs, and reports on Telegram. Plain software you can read and fork — no black box. Nombox is the maker; nombox is the service you'll spot in your process list — and yes, the *box suffix is the wink.
how.brain.title: samogrow service
how.brain.body: A small program that sends each photo to Claude, reads back the verdict, switches the light and pump plugs, and runs the Telegram bot. It is the only thing you maintain.
how.cloud.body: Claude reads each photo and returns a structured verdict; Telegram carries the daily digest, alerts, and your commands. Only the still image leaves your network — the camera is local RTSP, no cloud camera account.

how.flow: Each cycle: the brain grabs a snapshot, Claude returns a verdict, the brain switches the plugs within fixed safety caps, and the result lands in Telegram.
how.safety.body: The AI can request water; it cannot override the cap. Per-run and per-day pump caps, a bounded top-up jug (worst-case spill is just the jug's volume), and an optional float/leak sensor.
how.senses.body: The camera is the only automatic sensor — the AI's eyes. The EC/TDS meter and pH kit are handheld manual tools: you dip and read them yourself, and the AI only learns a value when you type it into Telegram. Continuous EC/pH/level probes exist but need a microcontroller — a natural add-on to the V5 Pi build, out of scope for the wiring-free versions. One gotcha with cheap TDS pens: the ×10 multiplier — “115 ×10” means 1,150 ppm; missing it burned our first plants, so always relay the true value.
how.schematic.alt: samogrow system schematic: an always-on machine runs the Bun brain, which talks to the Claude API and Telegram over the internet and, over home Wi-Fi, commands two Kasa smart plugs (light and top-up pump), a jug pump feeding the DWC tote, an always-on air pump, and a Tapo RTSP camera watching the plants.
how.schematic.cap: The same loop as a wiring-free system schematic — three network appliances, one laptop brain.
cost.title: What it costs
cost.sub: One price frame — a rough U.S. mid-2026 baseline, not a quote, and very much location-dependent: ~$255 for the manual build to start, ~$280 for the automated core, up to ~$335 with the water-safety add-ons. That is the same one-time bracket as the no-AI countertop units, while delivering the camera + AI capability that otherwise only ships on a $899 Gardyn with a ~$408/yr subscription.

cost.note: Nothing here is a black box: commodity seeds, code you can fork, and no vendor who can deprecate your garden or move the AI behind a paywall — the way AeroGarden owners were stranded when the company wound down and the app and pods went with it. The two-year math is just the receipt: ~$470 all-in, roughly $1,245 under Gardyn (the only commercial unit with real camera + AI) and below even a Click & Grow.

start.title: Quickstart — day one
start.sub: Want to try the software right now, before any parts arrive? Jump to step 3 — it runs the whole loop on your laptop with zero hardware.
start.fig.alt: Rendered mock-up of a finished samogrow build on a kitchen counter: a dark opaque tote of basil, parsley, cilantro and lettuce in net cups under two adjustable full-spectrum T5 strips, with a top-up water jug and pump, an air pump, a Wi-Fi camera, and two smart plugs.

step.1.title: Order parts & grab grown herbs
step.1.body: Fast path: all 10 core items are in one Amazon list — one click to cart the lot. Grab the tote and 2–4 healthy potted herbs (basil, parsley) locally from a garden center, ~$4–5 each — they're your day-one plants (no shipping wait).
step.2.title: Transplant → a full garden today
step.2.body: Nest each root ball in a net cup of clay pebbles, fill the reservoir, and you have a good-looking, working garden the same day — no germination wait. Heads up before you drop a plant in:
step.2.h1: Wash ALL the soil off the roots (lukewarm water, gently) — soil left in the reservoir rots and clogs. The one step you can't skip.
step.2.h2: Expect a few days of droop (transplant shock) — lower the light a bit; it recovers.
step.2.h3: Buy a plant, not a bunch. Get a potted herb plant from a nursery's seedling section (one plant in a 3–4" pot of soil), or search live herb plant online — not the produce-aisle “fresh herbs” packs, which are many weak seedlings crammed together (usable, but pull the clump apart into a few starts first).
step.2.h4: ⚠️ Feed to ~800–1,100 ppm — and read your TDS meter's ×10 flag. Cheap pens show 115 ×10 = 1,150 ppm, not 115. Miss that little multiplier and you'll dose ~10× and burn the plants — it happened to us (field-test log). Target on the display: 80–110 with ×10 lit.
step.3.title: Set up the software in practice mode
step.3.body: Get the program running on your computer and connect the Telegram bot, then test the whole loop against a sample photo — no devices needed yet.
step.4.title: Point it at the plants
step.4.body: Get the plugs and camera onto your Wi-Fi, aim the camera over the canopy, point the software at them, and set it to run on its own and restart itself.
start.seed.body: Prefer to grow from seed? Same build, lower cost — you just add ~2–4 weeks of germination before there's anything to transplant (parsley is the laggard at 10–28 days: soak 12–24 h, sow into moist rockwool, keep it warm). Garden-center pots beat crammed grocery “living herb” clumps; if you use those, split them gently.
start.harvest.body: Transplanted basil and mint are cuttable within days once they settle — expect a few days of transplant shock first. Parsley is the patient one. Lettuce bolts when it gets too warm.

inc.title: The incident blog
inc.sub: Real gardens produce real incidents, and we run them like production outages: dated, severity-tagged, blameless, and written up in public.
inc.i1.title: The ×10 incident — a tenfold nutrient overdose
inc.i1.story: The cheap TDS pen showed “115” and nobody noticed the tiny ×10 flag next to it. The reservoir was dosed as if the water were ten times cleaner than it was, and the salt concentration burned the plants within days.
inc.i1.impact: Impact: salt burn across the tote — necrotic mint, declining parsley; the most expensive lesson of the field test.
inc.i1.lesson: Lesson: always read the multiplier flag and relay true ppm; a units-validation step now guards every reported reading.
inc.i1.alt: Evidence photo from incident I-1: a handheld TDS meter held over the DWC reservoir reads 128 with the small ×10 multiplier flag lit — the reading that revealed the tenfold nutrient overdose.
inc.i1.cap: The smoking gun: 128 on the display, ×10 flag lit — 1,280 ppm in the reservoir.
inc.i3.title: The leafroller — a stowaway on a transplant
inc.i3.story: A caterpillar hitchhiked in on a garden-center transplant and spent two weeks eating mint by night, hiding in a silked rolled leaf by day. It was never seen in the act — the case was cracked from its droppings accumulating on the lid.
inc.i3.impact: Impact: one mint stem stripped bare, chewed mint and basil leaves; no plant lost.
inc.i3.lesson: Lesson: transplants import pests — inspect and quarantine new plants, and treat frass as a first-class alarm signal.
inc.i3.alt: Evidence photo from incident I-3: macro shot of black frass pellets — caterpillar droppings — scattered on the yellow reservoir lid, the clue that finally revealed the hidden leafroller.
inc.i3.cap: Not soil: frass on the lid — the droppings that gave the nocturnal caterpillar away.
inc.i5.title: Aphids the camera never saw
inc.i5.story: Sap-sucking aphids colonized the parsley and basil, cupping the basil's new growth. The automated camera checks are blind to pests this small — a hands-on leaf inspection found them, days after an early warning (“a few small flies”) went unacted-on.
inc.i5.impact: Impact: distorted basil growth and stippled parsley; recoverable, no plant lost.
inc.i5.lesson: Lesson: the camera is not a pest sensor — schedule human leaf checks, and act on small anomalies instead of filing them away.
inc.i5.alt: Evidence photo from incident I-5: close-up of grey-green aphids clustered along parsley stems and leaves, with fine pale stippling on the foliage.
inc.i5.cap: Aphid clusters on the parsley — invisible to the overhead camera, obvious in the hand.
inc.i6.title: Neem under the light — the self-inflicted burn
inc.i6.story: Treating the aphids, we sprayed neem oil once (~2026-08-15) with the grow light ON. Neem is phototoxic: oil film plus radiant light scorched the basil and mint. Damage surfaced 2026-08-18; the RCA landed 2026-08-20. The pest treatment worked — and caused the next incident.
inc.i6.impact: Impact: bronze necrotic patches on basil (worst) and mint; leaf-level only, recovering.
inc.i6.lesson: Lesson: lights OFF before spraying any oil — a hard precondition now written into the treatment guidance, not a footnote.
inc.i6.alt: Evidence photo from incident I-6: basil leaves with large bronze-brown necrotic scorch patches across the leaf surfaces — oil phototoxicity damage from a neem spray applied under the grow light.
inc.i6.cap: Bronze scorch on the basil, three days after a neem spray under a lit grow light.
